Discretionary vs. advisory | Julius Baer

Discretionary vs. advisory

April 15, 2019 by Elisabeth Yearley, Corporate Editor ) 2 min

The choice between taking investment decisions on your own or transferring the
responsibility to an investment professional sounds simple? In the opinion of
Daniel Obradovic (discretionary, left) and Mischa Anand (advisory, right), there
is more to it. In this article the two investment professionals share five aspects
to consider before taking the decision.

You have decided that now is the right time to start investing. Maybe you got that important
promotion (congratulations!), inherited wealth or simply rate your financial position as stable enough

to embark on this journey. The process that succeeds this decision is generally identical:

In a first step, your bank advisor will create a personal investment profile. It evaluates your financial
situation, investment objectives as well as prior knowledge and experience. Your investment guidelines
reflect your current understanding of financial instruments and the maximum amount of risk you are
able to take in order to attain your broader investment goals. Furthermore, an investment strategy is
defined. It serves as a guideline for adjusting your investments whenever your portfolio valuation

changes.

What is investment advice?
In our investment advice, we give you recommendations on finan­
cial instruments.
The following options are available:
–
Buy: We recommend that you buy a financial instrument.
–
Sale: We recommend that you sell a financial instrument.
–
Hold: We recommend that you do not sell a financial instru­
ment (but continue to hold it).
–
Do not buy: We recommend that you do not buy a financial
instrument.
As part of our investment advice, we take your financial situation
and your personal ideas into account. You will receive a declaration
of suitability from us with every consultation. This is a document in
which we explain how our recommendation suits you. In the end, you
decide for yourself whether you want to follow our recommendation.
Please note: Our recommendation is only valid at the time of the
consultation. We will only review the recommendation later if we
have agreed this with you in advance. If you have purchased finan­
cial instruments, you must therefore monitor their performance
yourself.

When providing advised services such as advisory mandates or
portfolio management mandates, Julius Baer has the duty by law
to consider that the products and financial instruments recom­
mended are suitable for the client. This means that a client has to
be able to adequately understand the underlying nature and risk
of a transaction or service and needs to have the ability to bear
any related financial loss. Julius Baer needs to assess whether the
transaction suits the client’s investment objectives.
To this end, Julius Baer is obliged to obtain specific information
about the client’s circumstances.
Where Julius Baer does not obtain the necessary information, it is
by law required to abstain from providing advised services.
Therefore, the provision of a duly signed “Client Investor Profile”
(CIP) is necessary for clients who would like to receive advised ser­
vices. This form is designed to evaluate the necessary information
regarding clients’,
–
knowledge and experience with regard to investment servic­
es and financial instruments;
–
investment goals, including investment purpose, planned
time horizon and risk appetite;

fessional client (‘per-se professional client’) or they
can apply for a change of classification (‘opting out’).
The following are defined by law as per-se professional clients:
• financial intermediaries as defined in the Swiss
Banking Act (BA), the Swiss Financial Institutions
Act (FinIA), and the Swiss Collective Investment
Schemes Act (CISA);
• insurance companies as defined in the
Swiss Insurance Supervision Act (ISA);
• foreign clients subject to prudential supervision;
• central banks;
• public entities with professional treasury
operations;
• pension funds and institutions dedicated to
occupational pension provision with professional
treasury;
• companies with professional treasury operations;
• large companies; and
• private investment structures with professional
treasury operations created for high-net-worth
private clients.

2
Per-se professional clients
Larger companies with a certain balance sheet or turn­
over size, many governmental or public bodies and fi­
nancial institutions, can qualify as per-se profession­
al clients. Such clients may indicate their eligibility to
Julius Baer, or Julius Baer may inform such clients that
it considers them to be eligible and intends to treat
them as a per-se professional client. Clients will be in­
formed in writing when Julius Baer considers the con­
ditions to be fulfilled, including information on rights of
protection that will no longer apply.

thorised financial institutions or certain governmen­
tal bodies such as central banks can be treated as an
eligible counterparty. Eligible counterparties have the
lowest level of consumer protection, as they are seen
as business-to-business clients. This status only applies
to non-advised services. In particular, the principles of
“best execution” do not apply to eligible counterparties.
4.3 Opting down
It is also possible for professional clients to request to be
treated as retail clients and receive a higher level of consum­

Clients must confirm that
they meet the necessary re­quirements in all aspects
before they can become professional clients. Clients
will be informed in ­writing when ­Julius Baer con­
siders the conditions to be fulfilled. Once this confirm­
ation is sent out, ­Julius Baer will henceforth treat
such clients as professional clients.
Regarding the offering of collective investment
schemes, professional clients as well as private clients
who have entered into a Discretionary or Advisory
Mandate Agreement are by law considered as qualified investors. This allows these clients to invest
in collective investment schemes that are offered to
qualified investors only. However, clients with an

collective investment schemes.

Clients who have been reclassified as professional
clients can decide at any time to opt into the private
client classification again.

results.question: Which factors does Julius Baer consider when determining the best possible result for a client?
results.expected_answer: price, cost, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size, and nature of the transaction or other relevant considerations
results.answer:
Julius Baer evaluates the following execution factors to achieve the best possible result for a client:  

- **Price** – the price at which the instrument is executed.  
- **Cost** – all fees and charges, including implicit market‑impact costs, external venue or clearing fees and Julius Baer’s own commissions/fees.  
- **Speed** – the time required to execute the transaction.  
- **Likelihood of execution and settlement** – the probability that the trade can be completed and settled.  
- **Size** – the transaction size and its effect on execution price.  
- **Nature of the transaction or any other relevant consideration** – characteristics of the trade that may affect execution.  

These factors are outlined in Julius Baer’s best‑execution framework[1][2].

a client to Julius Baer, such as advisory fees, custody

The most common form of compensation occurs
­between providers and distributors of financial instruments, whereby providers forward part of their rev­
enues from financial instruments to the distributor in
exchange for distribution services.
For example, in the area of investment funds, the
fund provider charges the investor a management
fee for managing the fund assets, which is disclosed
­in the fund prospectus. The fund provider may use
part of the revenues generated with this management fee to remunerate distributors such as banks
or financial advisors on an ongoing basis for access
to their distribution ­network, or for the administrative
efforts they need to undertake when distributing
the fund provider’s products. Fund providers may also

tended to enable all people, especially those with disabilities, to
access web content. The guidelines are based on four principles

Perceivability: As many people as possible should be able

is an alternative means of perception available, such as writ­

board.

able to read and understand the web content clearly. For ex­

able language whenever possible

–
Perceivability: As many people as possible should be able

Operability: As many people as possible should be able to
use the IT functions. This means, for example, that we en­
sure our web content can be operated using an ordinary key­
board.

ample, we offer our web content in simple and understand­

results.question: Which factors does Julius Baer consider for best execution?
results.expected_answer: price, cost, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size, and the nature of the transaction or other relevant considerations
results.answer:
Julius Baer evaluates the following factors when determining best execution for a client’s order:

* **Price** – the execution price of the instrument.  
* **Cost** – all fees and charges, including implicit market‑impact costs, external venue or brokerage fees and Julius Baer’s own commissions.  
* **Speed** – the time required to complete the transaction.  
* **Likelihood of execution and settlement** – the probability that the trade can be fully executed and settled.  
* **Size** – the transaction size and its effect on execution price.  
* **Nature of the transaction or any other relevant consideration** – characteristics of the specific order that may affect execution.  

These factors are set out in Julius Baer’s best‑execution framework[1][2].

INDUCEMENTS
2.1
What are inducements?
Inducements are monetary or non-monetary benefits a
Julius Baer entity may receive from another legal entity (in­
cl. Group companies), which are not paid directly by a cli­
ent or on behalf of a client. Charges paid directly by the
client to Julius Baer, such as advisory fees, custody fees or
transaction fees (including transaction fees that are includ­
ed in the issue price of an instrument) are not inducements.
The most common form of inducement occurs between
providers and distributors of financial instruments, whereby
product providers forward part of their revenues from prod­
uct internal charges to the distributor in exchange for distri­
bution services.
For example, in the area of investment funds, the fund pro­
vider charges the investor a management fee for managing
the fund assets, which is disclosed in the fund prospectus.
The fund provider may use part of the revenues generated
with this management fee to remunerate distributors such
as banks or financial advisers for access to their distribution
network, or for the administrative efforts they need to un­
dertake when distributing the fund provider’s products.

Non-monetary benefits may occur in the form of informa­
tion on financial instruments, participation in conferences,
and hospitality etc.
2.2 Regulation of inducements
Because inducements can lead to potential conflicts of interest,
their reception and payment is strictly regulated. Clients must
be properly informed about their existence and receive prop­
er reports about inducements that have occurred. For the ser­
vice of portfolio management, the reception of inducements is
strictly prohibited. In some countries, the reception of induce­
ments is also prohibited for other types of investment services
such as investment advice or even non-advised transactions.
Where inducements are allowed, investment firms must make
sure that they do not impair the objectivity of their advice, and
that they contribute to a tangible benefit for the client.
2.3 Inducements received by Julius Baer
The Julius Baer entities covered in this brochure offer solely
inducement-free discretionary portfolio management man­
dates. Within the scope of an advisory agreement, they rec­
ommend only inducement-free products, unless explicitly
agreed otherwise with the client in the advisory agreement.

They may receive inducements in connection with prod­
ucts held or purchased at the initiative of the client (unless
in countries where inducements are generally prohibited or
where such products are not part of the offering).
Where Julius Baer receives inducements, it makes sure that
they do not impair its duty to act in accordance with the best
rendered objective advice, but rather contribute to a tangi­
ble benefit for the client, such as a higher level of service.
The acceptance of non-monetary benefits by individual em­
ployees is further clearly regulated by an internal policy and
undergoes a strict approval process.
2.4 Calculation of inducements
The amount of inducements depends on the financial instru­
ment, its provider and the volume of assets invested in the
financial instrument. The maximum bandwidths are detailed
below:
Distribution fees from investment fund providers (in % of in­
vestment volume p.a.)
–
Money market funds: up to 0.5 %
–
Bond funds: up to 1.0 %
–
Equity funds: up to 2.0 %
–
Other funds: up to 2.0 %
–
Non-traditional funds: up to 2.0 %

on the bond market, the price you pay for a bond may be more
or less than the nominal value. There are several reasons why the

–
If a bond is issued with a fixed interest rate of, say, 8 % and

The reverse is also true. If interest rates rise, the fixed rate of

might fall. On the other hand, the company’s rating may be
improved leading to a price rise.
–
The inflation rate might start to creep up and the interest
rate on some bonds might start to look less attractive com­
pared with other investments.

–
interest rate risk – the risk that bond prices will fall as inter­
est rates rise. By buying a bond, the bondholder has com­
mitted to receiving a fixed rate of return for a fixed period.
Should the market interest rate rise from the date of the
bond’s purchase, the bond’s price will fall accordingly. The
bond will then be trading at a discount to reflect the lower
return that an investor will make on the bond. Market inter­

for, and supply of, money in the economy, the inflation rate,
the stage that the business cycle is in, as well as the govern­
ment’s monetary and fiscal policies;

able bonds have call provisions, which allow the bond issuer
to purchase the bond back from the bondholders and retire
the issue. This is usually done when interest rates have fallen
substantially since the issue date. Call provisions allow

Discretionary vs. advisory

April 15, 2019 by Elisabeth Yearley, Corporate Editor ) 2 min

The choice between taking investment decisions on your own or transferring the
responsibility to an investment professional sounds simple? In the opinion of
Daniel Obradovic (discretionary, left) and Mischa Anand (advisory, right), there
is more to it. In this article the two investment professionals share five aspects
to consider before taking the decision.

You have decided that now is the right time to start investing. Maybe you got that important
promotion (congratulations!), inherited wealth or simply rate your financial position as stable enough

to embark on this journey. The process that succeeds this decision is generally identical:

What is investment advice?
In our investment advice, we give you recommendations on finan­
cial instruments.
The following options are available:
–
Buy: We recommend that you buy a financial instrument.
–
Sale: We recommend that you sell a financial instrument.
–
Hold: We recommend that you do not sell a financial instru­
ment (but continue to hold it).
–
Do not buy: We recommend that you do not buy a financial
instrument.
As part of our investment advice, we take your financial situation
and your personal ideas into account. You will receive a declaration
of suitability from us with every consultation. This is a document in
which we explain how our recommendation suits you. In the end, you
decide for yourself whether you want to follow our recommendation.
Please note: Our recommendation is only valid at the time of the
consultation. We will only review the recommendation later if we
have agreed this with you in advance. If you have purchased finan­
cial instruments, you must therefore monitor their performance
yourself.

Discretionary vs. advisory | Julius Baer

investment advisor like Mischa Anand, is placed at your side to discuss all investment-related

on your behalf. Both options come with advantages and disadvantages. It depends on your personal

YEFI also connects farmers to ethical

The Young Emerging Farmers Initiative (YEFI) is the first organ-
isation in Zambia dedicated exclusively to the needs of young
farmers aged 15 to 35, a generation that is central to the future
of the country’s food systems yet often overlooked by main-
stream agricultural support. YEFI strengthens the resilience of
young small-scale farmers by promoting restorative farming
practices and improving their access to markets. Through its No
Agrochem project, young farmers receive training in agroeco-
logical methods that protect ecosystems, restore degraded soils
and respond to growing demand for high-quality food.

In Zambia, smallholder farmers who grow most of the country’s
food are caught in a difficult cycle: dependent on synthetic
fertilisers that degrade their soil and drain their income, yet excluded from the markets that could offer an alternative. YEFI
is breaking this cycle – training young farmers in agroecology and
connecting them to buyers who value sustainably produced food.
“Before, I was spending over 1,800
kwacha every season on syn-
thetic fertilisers, and my yields
were still poor.

The
ambition goes beyond individual farms:
by building market linkages, influencing
policy, and anchoring knowledge in
local communities, YEFI is laying the
groundwork for a food system that is both
ecologically sound and economically fair.
“YEFI illustrates how connecting knowledge, resources and opportunity can
create the conditions for young farmers
to build sustainable livelihoods on their
own terms.”
Ariane de Lannoy
Julius Baer Foundation Board Member
Why does it work?
• Local solutions replace costly inputs
Farmers learn to produce their own fertiliser and
pesticides from locally available materials, elimi-
nating dependency on expensive agrochemicals.
• Market access for marginalised producers
YEFI connects smallholders to ethical buyers, re-
tailers and cooperatives – building fair value
chains where sustainably grown food finds reliable
demand.
• Youth-led change from farm to policy
As a youth-led organisation, YEFI ensures that
young farmers are not only practitioners, but
also become advocates with a seat at the policy
table – shaping Zambia’s national agroecol-
ogy strategy and building a movement for lasting
food system transformation.

YEFI’s
food-system approach reinforces community networks, connects
producers with buyers and contributes to an enabling policy
environment.
Rainforest Alliance, Colombia & Peru (2025–2028)
The Rainforest Alliance is a global organisation working at the
intersection of environmental sustainability and rural livelihoods.
This project strengthens the organisational, economic and
productive capacities of small-scale coffee and cacao farmers in
the Amazon Basin of Colombia and Peru. Sustainable agriculture
in this biodiversity-rich region supports livelihoods and forest
conversation. With a particular emphasis on including women,
young people and indigenous communities, the initiative promotes
the adoption of climate-smart, regenerative farming practices.
It also improves farmers’ access to credit and supports the instal-
lation of new infrastructure, such as cacao drying and fermen-
tation facilities. Together, these efforts aim to empower previously
underserved groups to increase their yields and meet the stan-
dards required to access more profitable international markets.

Continuity through change
Over six decades, the context in which the Foundation
operates has evolved considerably. Family dy-
namics shift across generations, and governance
structures become more formalised and professional.
Leadership transitions have also taken place,
including the moment when family members entrusted
the Foundation’s leadership to a carefully selected
group of Bank executives and industry experts along
side the family executives.
As society and contexts evolve, a foundation must
adjust accordingly. Strategic priorities are refined,
operational approaches develop and management
structures mature. Such evolution is not a depar-
ture from legacy; it is part of preserving it.

bringing people together across

co-funding with others, recognising that complex
challenges are best addressed together.

mentorship, and enabling young farmers in Zambia
to adopt sustainable practices while connecting

from them.

As well as introducing a dizzying array of new applications and possibilities, the

held assumptions, their role is one that depends heavily on people.

ML engineers are in high demand - and the reasons are clear. Artificial intelligence, of which ML is one

A culture of openness and experimentation

purpose-driven, client-focused approach. “The relationship managers are interested and open enough
